rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Slide/lecture headers pass the squint test AND the truth clause.
rules_evaluated.evidence: Harm the rule prevents: a cold self-study reader (or a fast operator scanning the deck) hits a header that could belong to any exercise and gets no orientation from it. Five of six `##` headers pass cleanly — 'Read the ticket for your bug' (L11), 'Read the conventions off the ticket' (L20), 'Write the close-out and send it' (L33), 'Double-check the voice' (L41) each name the one concrete action; 'Anything can be reverse-engineered' (L45) is a claim-header the body immediately supports ('Anything can be inspected and reverse-engineered with an LLM...'). The sixth, '## What happened' (L50), is the rule's own listed failure shape verbatim — 'empty containers... head anything and name nothing.' I checked the corpus for precedent: `grep -rl '^## What happened' curriculum/exercises/*.md` → this file only, out of 34 other exercise files (real command, this session). Every other exercise's closing header names something specific ('Take stock of the loop you ran', 'Ship the PR', 'Carry the plan forward', 'Take the context move past this site'...) — 'What happened' is the corpus's sole generic recap label, not an established convention this file follows. Harm is present but mild, not severe: the section is the file's terminal beat, its two-sentence body ('Two things came out of one ticket...') is read immediately regardless of the header's specificity, and no mid-exercise navigation depends on this label. Per the template's default ('Other rules are TODO unless severe'), filed non-blocking.
